subject: Leap second
hook: LEAP SECOND IS NOT WHAT YOU THINK
angle: Leap seconds are not added because the Earth is slowing down. Between 1972 and 2016, the Earth's rotation actually sped up overall, yet 27 leap seconds were added simply because each day was still slightly longer than an exact 86,400 atomic seconds.
angle_support: It is a mistake, however, to consider leap seconds as indicators of a slowing of Earth's rotation rate; more properly, they are indicators of the accumulated difference between atomic time and time measured by Earth rotation.

The plot at the top of this section shows that in 1972 the average length of day was approximately 86400.003 seconds and in 2016 it was approximately 86400.001 seconds, indicating an overall increase in Earth's rotation rate over that time period.
title: Why Leap Seconds Don't Mean Earth Is Slowing Down
description: Most people assume leap seconds are added because Earth's rotation is steadily slowing. In reality, our planet actually spun faster over the decades leap seconds were introduced. The adjustment exists only because our atomic definition of a day is slightly shorter than a solar one.
narration: LEAP SECOND IS NOT WHAT YOU THINK You picture our planet grinding to a halt, forcing us to pause our clocks. But between 1972 and 2016, Earth's rotational spin actually accelerated overall. Yet timekeepers still inserted twenty-seven leap seconds. That is because an average solar day remained roughly one to three milliseconds longer than exactly eighty-six thousand four hundred atomic seconds. Even while accelerating, that surplus kept accumulating. We were never measuring planetary fatigue, just an ancient, slightly oversized day.
